opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things where your low-dimensional intuition just completely fails you.

Suppose you have an image classifier and some input it labels "cat." In a million-dimensional space, there's almost always some direction where moving a tiny distance, small enough that a human sees no change, flips the label to "guacamole" or whatever. So the boundary is really close.

But if you pick a random direction and walk along it, you usually have to go a long way before anything changes. You can add a lot of random noise to an image and the classifier is fine. So how can the boundary be both close and far?

The answer is that the boundary isn't close in every direction. It's close in a very small number of directions relative to the total dimensionality. Imagine the boundary near your point is roughly a hyperplane. The distance along a direction depends on the cosine between that direction and the normal to the plane. In high dimensions, a random unit vector has a cosine with any fixed vector of roughly one over the square root of d. With a million dimensions, that's about one in a thousand. So you'd need to travel around a thousand times farther along a random direction than along the worst-case direction to cross the boundary.

That's the core geometric fact. Random directions are almost orthogonal to everything, including the one direction you care about. The small adversarial perturbation is out there, but it occupies a vanishingly small fraction of the sphere of possible directions. Random search essentially never hits it.

This is why gradient-based attacks work so well. The gradient tells you, more or less, which direction points toward the boundary. You're not sampling the sphere, you're being pointed at the needle in the haystack. It's also why defenses that only test robustness to random noise are misleading. Being robust to Gaussian noise of some magnitude tells you almost nothing about worst-case robustness, because you're measuring in the directions that didn't matter.

There's a nice way to see it as a picture. The classifier's regions aren't round blobs with the data point in the middle. They're more like thin slabs or pancakes. Along most axes you can go a long way, but along a few axes the wall is right there. In a million dimensions, "a few axes" is almost none of them, so if you search randomly you conclude the model is robust, and if you search adversarially you conclude it's extremely brittle. Both are true. They're just answering different questions.

r001.rationale: The response relates distance to the boundary to the cosine with its normal and contrasts random travel with a worst-case direction, but it does not clearly identify the perpendicular-to-the-boundary direction as the shortest route.

r002.rationale: It explains that random directions are nearly orthogonal to the direction toward the boundary, so travel along them must be much longer and random search is unlikely to find the nearby boundary.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that sounds paradoxical until you actually sit down and think about the geometry, and then it becomes almost obvious. Let me try to walk through how I think about it.

The thing to remember is that the picture everyone has in their head is a two-dimensional picture. You've got a point, there's a decision boundary somewhere nearby, and if the boundary is close, well, in 2D "close" means you'll stumble into it pretty quickly if you just wander around. There are only so many directions to go. That intuition is completely wrong in high dimensions, and it's wrong in a way that matters.

So take an ImageNet-sized image. You're in something like a hundred-and-fifty-thousand-dimensional space. Now suppose there's a direction, one specific direction, where if you move a tiny distance, say an epsilon that no human could perceive, you cross the decision boundary and the classifier flips from "panda" to "gibbon." That's the adversarial example. The boundary really is close along that direction.

But here's the key fact: when you pick a random direction in a hundred-and-fifty-thousand dimensions, it's almost exactly orthogonal to any fixed direction you care about. That's just concentration of measure. The dot product between a random unit vector and your adversarial direction is going to be on the order of one over the square root of the dimension. So if you walk a distance epsilon in a random direction, the component of that step along the direction that actually matters is something like epsilon divided by, I don't know, four hundred. Essentially nothing. You've moved almost entirely along directions that the classifier doesn't care about.

Another way to say it is that the decision boundary near a data point isn't shaped like a wall right next to you. It's more like you're in a really thin, really long, almost flat valley. In most directions the boundary is extremely far away. In a small number of directions it's extremely close. And "a small number" in high-dimensional space is still a vanishingly small fraction of the total volume of directions you could pick. So random search spends basically all of its time probing the directions where nothing happens.

This is also, incidentally, why random noise doesn't fool classifiers. If you add Gaussian noise to an image, you're sampling a random direction, and the model is totally fine with that. That's exactly the robustness that people would point to and say "look, the model is robust to perturbations." And it is, to random perturbations. It's just that random perturbations and worst-case perturbations are completely different things in high dimensions, and the gap between them grows with dimension.

So what does this mean for actually finding the boundary? It means you need the gradient, or something that approximates it. The gradient tells you exactly which direction the loss changes fastest, which is precisely the one direction out of a hundred and fifty thousand that random search would almost never pick. That's why white-box attacks are so cheap and why they work in a handful of steps. And it's why, when you go to the black-box setting and you don't have gradients, the entire game becomes about estimating that direction efficiently. You can do finite differences, which costs you one query per dimension, which is horrible, or you can be cleverer and use the fact that the useful directions tend to be somewhat low-dimensional and structured, which is where a lot of the query-efficient attack work comes from.

The thing I'd push back on, if someone takes the naive version of this, is the claim that this means adversarial examples are somehow "unnatural" or just a weird artifact of looking really hard. I actually don't think that's the right takeaway. The boundary being hard to find at random doesn't mean it isn't there, and it doesn't mean the model has learned the thing you wanted it to learn. It means that evaluating robustness by throwing random noise at a model tells you almost nothing about what an adversary can do. Those are different questions, and conflating them is one of the most common mistakes I see.

r001.rationale: The response describes a direction that crosses the boundary, but does not identify it as perpendicular to a nearby planar boundary or as the shortest route to that boundary.

r002.rationale: It explains that random directions are nearly orthogonal to the relevant direction, so a random step has only a tiny component toward the boundary.

astra-6.text:
The key is that the distance to the boundary and the probability of finding it in a random direction are different things. Imagine, just locally, that the decision boundary is a flat plane. There’s a direction perpendicular to that plane that gets you across it with a very small change. But if you pick a random direction in a high-dimensional space, it’s almost orthogonal to that perpendicular direction. Most of your movement is going sideways, rather than toward the boundary.

More quantitatively, in d dimensions, a random unit vector typically has a component of about one over the square root of d along any particular direction. So even if the boundary is only epsilon away, you might have to travel on the order of epsilon times the square root of d to reach it along a random direction, assuming you’re going toward it at all.

That’s why random perturbations can make a classifier look robust even when a very small adversarial perturbation exists. An optimization-based attack uses information about the model to find a direction that actually moves toward the boundary. Random search mostly spends its effort moving in directions that don’t help.

r001.rationale: It describes the perpendicular direction to the locally flat boundary as the direction that crosses it with a very small change, communicating the shortest route.

r002.rationale: It says random directions are almost orthogonal to the direction toward the boundary, so movement is mostly sideways and reaching it can require roughly ε√d distance.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that distance to the boundary and the probability of finding it in a random direction are different things. Imagine, locally, that the decision boundary is a flat plane. There’s one direction perpendicular to that plane that takes you straight to it. But in a high-dimensional space, a random direction is almost perpendicular to that particular direction. So you can move quite a long way and make very little progress toward the boundary.

If the boundary is a distance epsilon away, the component of a random unit vector toward it is typically on the order of one over the square root of the dimension. So you might need to travel roughly epsilon times the square root of the dimension to reach it, even though a carefully chosen perturbation only needs to travel epsilon.

That’s why adding random noise and seeing that the classifier is fine doesn’t tell you there aren’t adversarial examples nearby. An attack uses information about the model to find a direction that changes the decision, and random search is very unlikely to line up with that direction.

r001.rationale: It says the direction perpendicular to the locally flat boundary takes you straight to it, and contrasts that with a carefully chosen perturbation of length epsilon.

r002.rationale: It explains that a random direction is nearly perpendicular to the direction toward the boundary, so its component toward the boundary is small and it makes little progress.
